Q: How to avoid page rendering delays in PHP and JavaScript web development? A:

A would advise against mindless caching. As a part of wider approach of optimizing something that is not slow. Instead, profile your app first, then optimize the actual bottleneck, for which caching would be just one of many strategies

Q: I am completely new to coding and looking for advice A:

I would recommend

  1. Learn and practice algorithms on Leetcode as it helps build strong fundamentals and is critical for interviews

  2. Pick up a small project that is fun and useful, leverage AI tools like Copilot to build it, to gain familiarity with tooling and real-world intuition

  3. Read popular books like Effective Java by Joshua Block or Clean Coder by Robert Martin to strengthen theoretical knowledge

Q: When to use forwarding and when to use stalls to handle data hazards in pipelining (RISC V architecture) A:

Forwarding is always preferred over a stall, because forwarding is "free" whereas a stall costs a cycle, slowing execution.

In the case of use-after-load, both forwarding and a stall are used.  If no forwarding were used, then that scenario will require 2 stall cycles between the load and the immediately following use.  When forwarding is used, only one stall cycle is needed for that.

The general concept is that instructions write to the register file and read from the register file, and that is how prior instructions share results with subsequent ones.  But the writing happens in the WB stage, and the reading in the ID stage.  This means that by the time a first instruction accomplishes its WB, a second instruction has already done its ID stage (register reads), 2 cycles prior.  This is why 2 cycle stall would be indicated for your use-after-load scenario.

(As a technical note, an ID read of the same register can be made to read the result being written in WB of the same register in the same cycle.  If this were not the case, then a 3 cycle stall would be needed to share results from back-to-back instructions, as the latter instruction would have to wait for the WB of the former to finish before starting its ID.  Some call this (ability to overlap ID and WB) an internal forward in the register file itself, others say half cycles can be used, and yet still I maintain that this is a logical consequence of writing and reading the same register at the same time, given how circuitry settles values.)

A forward is possible, to avoid using a stall, when the data value of interest is available somewhere in the processor, despite not yet written to the register file.  It takes some comparators in the appropriate places, that override the ID-read value with the proper value from the place it is available.

So, in the case of add-followed-by-add, the result of the first addition is available immediately after the EX stage of the first instruction (yet won't be written to the register file for 2 more cycles), and, the second instruction will execute EX in that very next cycle.  So, the forward detects that the second instruction's ID stage read has obtained a stale value, and that should be replaced by the first instruction's computational result.  Thus, an EX-output to EX-input forward is used and avoids a stall (also called simply: EX to EX forward).  Were no forward used, a 2 (or 3) cycle stall would be needed as per above discussion.

In the case of use-after-load, the load result doesn't become available inside the processor until after the memory (DM) stage for the load instructions.  But the second instruction needs it by the EX stage.  So, the best we can do is a forward from DM-output to EX-input, plus a stall of the second instruction to wait for the DM-output to happen before doing its EX stage.

Q: Can I use regular expressions to search for multiples of a number? A:

I checked the first 48^4 (~5.3mn) multiples of 48. Here are select distributions

mod % 72 :: multiples of 24

  1          1769472  0
  2          1769472 24
  3          1769472 48



 1            589824 0
 2            589824 24
 3            589824 48
 4            589824 72
 5            589824 96
 6            589824 120
 7            589824 144
 8            589824 168
 9            589824 192

mod % 40 :: multiples of 8

  1          1061683  0
  2          1061684  8
  3          1061683 16
  4          1061683 24
  5          1061683 32

mod % 88 :: also multiples of 8

   1              482583  0
   2              482584  8
   3              482583 16
   4              482583 24
   5              482583 32
   6              482583 40
   7              482584 48
   8              482584 56
   9              482583 64
  10              482583 72
  11              482583 80

mod % 80 :: multiples of 16

  1          1061683 0
  2          1061683 16
  3          1061683 32
  4          1061684 48
  5          1061683 64

mod % 84 :: multiples of 12

  1           758345  0
  2           758345 12
  3           758345 24
  4           758345 36
  5           758346 48
  6           758345 60
  7           758345 72

but in decimal, some interesting patterns emerge when checking last 3 digits (zero-padded below) :

  • among zero-padded 3 digits those ending in 2 or 6 - the middle digit must be *ODD
    • When grouping middle digit by [37] v. [159], only 4 groups show up in a related but non-overlapping fashion :
  [ 02468 ] [  3 7  ] [2]
  [ 13579 ] [  3 7  ] [6] 
  [ 13579 ] [ 1 5 9 ] [2]
  [ 02468 ] [ 1 5 9 ] [6]

  • among zero-padded 3 digits those ending in 0 4 or 8 — the middle digit must be *EVEN

    • When grouping middle digit by [26] v. [0248], only 4 groups show up in a related but non-overlapping fashion :
  [ 02468 ] [  2 6  ]  [4]
  [ 13579 ] [  2 6  ] [08]
  [ 13579 ] [ 0 4 8 ]  [4]
  [ 02468 ] [ 0 4 8 ] [08]

putting it all together, I'm getting ...

 [02468]([048][0 8]|[159][6]|[26][ 4 ]|[37][2])
 [13579]([048][ 4 ]|[159][2]|[26][0 8]|[37][6])

with a 100 % match rate against actuals

 jot 5308416 48 - 48 | 

 mawk '/(^|[^0-9])(0+|48|96|[0-9]*([02468]([048][08]|[159]6|[26]4|
           [37]2)|[13579]([048]4|[159]2|[26][08]|[37]6)))([^0-9]|$)/'

 out9: 48.4MiB 0:00:02 [19.8MiB/s] [19.8MiB/s] [ <=>]

 rows       = 5308416 | UTF8 chars = 50769348 | bytes      = 50769348

Among all even numbers up to the same upper limit of 254,803,968, the regex filter keeps 1 in 4 numbers. Among the kept population, the actual multiples of 48 account for 1 in 6.

Obviously this isn't all that tight of a criteria since it's only last 3 decimal digits, but at least there weren't any false negatives (someone can go make it sign aware if they like)

Q: CIDER: do not run removed test A:

Commenting out or removing the test doesn’t remove it from the namespace in the running process. Rather than taking out the complete deftest just empty out the body (so nothing is tested) and eval that.

Then you can remove it if you like. It’ll still appear in the running tests for this session but there’s nothing in it, it’ll pass, so it won’t bother you.

Q: Medical image processing feature descriptors A:

Yes, many “classic” computer vision descriptors like SIFT, SURF, HOG, and LBP are widely used in medical image processing, especially when data is limited or interpretability matters. In fields such as podiatric imaging (e.g., diabetic foot ulcer assessment, plantar tissue analysis, thermal foot scans), these hand‑crafted descriptors are commonly applied to capture texture, edge patterns, shape, and local intensity variations rather than generic object features. Beyond those, medical imaging often relies on texture‑focused descriptors like Gray Level Co‑occurrence Matrix (GLCM) features, Wavelet‑based features, Gabor filters, and Fractal features, since biological tissues tend to show subtle texture changes rather than strong geometric corners. These descriptors are especially useful for tasks like ulcer detection, tissue degeneration analysis, and inflammation mapping, where explainability is important for clinicians. While deep learning features dominate recent work, traditional local and global descriptors are still very relevant in medical domains due to smaller datasets, regulatory needs, and clinical interpretability, and they are often combined with ML classifiers in real‑world medical systems.
